lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** is a mass attached to a spring. It vibrates because each part behaves in its own way.
children: Spring: **The spring tends to return to its equilibrium position** (its normal resting length). If it is stretched or compressed, it pulls or pushes to get back to that length.
Mass: **A moving mass tends to keep moving**, so once it starts moving, it does not stop by itself.

When the mass is pulled out and released, the spring pulls it back toward equilibrium. The mass is still moving when it reaches equilibrium, so it **keeps going** past that point and compresses the spring.
The compressed spring then pushes the mass back the other way. The mass overshoots again, and the cycle repeats. This repeating back-and-forth movement is called **vibration**.
On a real table, **friction** slowly stops the motion. The model leaves friction out, so in the model the system vibrates forever.

teaching.text: The same system can move in **two directions**. It is important to understand both, because some systems are easier to think about in one direction than the other.
children: Longitudinal motion: The mass moves **left and right**, back and forth along the line of the spring.
Transverse motion: The mass sits between **two walls** with a spring on each side, and it moves **up and down**, across the line of the springs.

teaching.text: **Both kinds of motion work the same way, for the same reason.** When the transverse mass is pulled up, the springs **get stretched**. Springs pull back when they are stretched, so they pull the mass back down. When the mass passes the middle, the springs are not stretched at all. But the mass is still moving, so it keeps going and stretches the springs on the other side.
children: Both versions vibrate at the **same rate**, because they have the same mass and the same springs pulling them back.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Frequency** is the number of back-and-forth cycles a system completes each second. Two things control it, the **mass** and the **stiffness**. Each one has the same effect in longitudinal and in transverse motion.
Mass and stiffness change the frequency in opposite directions.
children: Mass: **A heavier mass vibrates more slowly.** A heavy mass is hard to start and hard to turn around, so each cycle takes longer. For example, **heavy branches sway slowly, while small branches sway quickly.** Making the mass **four times heavier cuts the frequency in half**.

Stiffness: **A stiffer spring makes the system vibrate faster.** A stiffer spring pulls back with more force, so it turns the mass around sooner. Making the spring **four times stiffer doubles the frequency**.

teaching.text: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.** But each part only affects the frequency while it is actually doing its job.
children: **A mass affects the frequency only when it moves, and a spring affects the frequency only when it stretches or compresses.** If a mass never moves, it could be made a thousand pounds heavier without changing the frequency. If a spring never stretches, it adds no stiffness.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: A system with **two masses** has two walls, one spring from each wall to a mass, and **one spring between the two masses**. All the masses are equal, and all the springs are equally stiff. This system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**. **A mode is simply one way that a system can vibrate.**
children: Mode 1: The masses move **together**. If both masses are pulled up and released, they rise and fall side by side. In longitudinal motion, they move left and right as a pair.

Mode 2: The masses move **against each other**. If one mass is pulled down and the other up, then whenever one rises, the other falls. In longitudinal motion, they move toward each other and then apart.

A system can also vibrate in **both modes at the same time**. If both masses are pulled up, but one higher than the other, they move together and against each other at once. Real movements, including speech, do this all the time.

teaching.text: **When the masses move together, they go back and forth slowly. When they move against each other, they go back and forth quickly.** So **Mode 2 has the higher frequency**. Both modes use the same masses and the same springs, so to explain the difference, look at **what each spring is doing**.
children: Mode 1: The middle spring is never stretched or compressed. It is carried along like a solid bar, so **Mode 1 effectively uses only two springs**.
Mode 2: The middle spring is stretched and compressed repeatedly. **All three springs are working**, so Mode 2 has three springs' worth of stiffness instead of two.
**More stiffness means a stronger pull back toward equilibrium, and a stronger pull means a higher frequency.** A higher mode does not use stiffer springs. It makes the same springs stretch more.

teaching.text: This leads to a general rule. **The more the masses move against each other, the more the springs stretch and compress. That gives the mode more stiffness, so it has a higher frequency.** This is why a system with several masses has several frequencies. It has several modes, and each higher mode is stiffer than the one before it.

sections.title: Pop quiz

teaching.text: Adding a third mass adds a third way to vibrate, so **a system with three masses has three modes**. You can tell the modes apart the same way as before, by asking which masses move together and which move against each other.
children: Together: All three masses move back and forth together.
Outer masses opposed: The two outer masses move against each other while the middle mass stays still.
Middle opposed: The middle mass moves against the two outer masses.
The more the masses move against each other, the more the springs stretch. So these three modes go from the lowest frequency to the highest.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses** and four springs, the system has **three modes**, and each mode has its own frequency.
children: Mode 1: All three masses move back and forth **together**. This mode has the **lowest frequency**, because the two middle springs are carried along and add no stiffness.

Mode 2: The **middle mass stays still** while the two outer masses move against each other. This mode has the **middle frequency**. It is started by pulling the outer masses apart carefully without touching the middle one.

Mode 3: The **middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses**, so **every mass moves against its neighbors**. This mode has the most stretching and compressing, the most stiffness, and the **highest frequency**.

teaching.text: A mass only affects the frequency when it moves. So **changing one mass only changes the modes where that mass moves**. If the **middle mass is made heavier**, the frequency of **Mode 1 and Mode 3 goes down**, because the middle mass moves in both of those modes. **Mode 2 does not change**, because the middle mass does not move at all in Mode 2.
All three modes can also happen **at the same time**. However the system is started, its motion is a mix of these three **pure modes**.
children: **Learning a musical instrument means learning how to make its masses and springs vibrate in certain modes and not others.** How a string is plucked or a violin is bowed determines which modes start vibrating, and the strongest modes are what we hear as **notes**.
A **trained singer** does the same thing with the vocal folds. The singer controls the mass and stiffness of the folds well enough to sing in tune.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The same pattern works for any number of masses. **N masses give N modes**, so one mass has one way to vibrate, two masses have two, and six masses have six. Higher modes have **more reversals**, which are places where neighboring masses move in opposite directions. More reversals mean more stretching, so **higher modes have higher frequencies**.
children: In a chain of separate masses like this, the mode frequencies are usually **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: Each mode has the same basic shape no matter how many masses are in the chain.
children: Mode 1: **Every Mode 1 looks alike**, because all the masses move up and down together.
Mode 2: **Every Mode 2 looks alike**, because the **left side moves against the right side**. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
Mode 3: **Every Mode 3 looks alike**, because the **middle moves against the sides**.
Four masses: The four modes are all four together, the left pair against the right pair, the middle pair against the outer pair, and every mass against its neighbors.

teaching.text: Adding more and more masses and springs, all the way to an **infinite number**, produces a **string**, like a guitar or piano string. **Every tiny piece of a string has mass, and every tiny piece stretches like a spring**, so a string has an infinite number of modes.
children: In the **lowest mode**, the whole string moves up and down together with almost no stretching between its pieces, so this mode gives the **lowest note**.
In each higher mode, more parts of the string move against each other. A string that is plucked carelessly vibrates in many modes at once.

A **building** is like a string that is fixed to the ground at the bottom and free to sway at the top. Engineers design buildings to sway only in **Mode 1**, because in higher modes some floors would move one way while other floors moved the other way.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Take a **string fixed at both ends** whose lowest mode vibrates at **100 hertz**, which means 100 times per second. Its next modes vibrate at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**. These frequencies are **whole-number multiples** of the lowest one, and modes that line up this way are called **harmonics**.
children: Each higher mode completes more cycles in the same amount of time. These are **consecutive harmonics**, which means both the odd and the even multiples are included.

teaching.text: The even spacing comes from the way each mode is built from copies of the first mode. **Mode 1 is a single bump.** **Mode 2 is two copies of that bump**, with one half moving up while the other half moves down.
children: Because Mode 2 has two copies, it has **twice the stiffness** of Mode 1, so it has twice the frequency. Mode 3 has three copies, and the fifth mode has **five copies of the first mode**.
So if the lowest mode is 200 hertz, the fifth mode is five times 200, which is 1000 hertz.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in **all of its modes at the same time**. When the separate motions are added together, the string makes one complicated, changing shape. A **spectrum** shows **which frequencies are in a sound and how strong each one is**. **Frequency** goes along the horizontal axis, and **amplitude**, which is strength, goes up the vertical axis.
children: For a string moving in all five modes, the spectrum has **five evenly spaced spikes**. In this example, the spikes have **equal height**, because nothing has filtered the sound.
If the string vibrated **only in Mode 3**, the spectrum would have **one spike at the Mode 3 frequency** and nothing else. This is like a **one-hot encoding**, where only one slot is on.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are more complicated than strings.** They are a sheet of muscle, which is called a **membrane**. So their masses and springs are spread across a surface instead of along a line. The same ideas about modes still apply.
children: Mode 1: The whole surface moves up and down together.
Mode 2: The **left half moves against the right half**.
Mode 3: The surface is divided in the other direction, so the two halves on either side of a still line move against each other.
Mode 4: Four sections move against each other, and higher modes become more and more complicated.
Each mode is labeled with a pair of numbers. The first counts how many bumps fit along the length, and the second counts how many fit across the width.

teaching.text: In real vocal folds, **all the modes happen at the same time**, so voicing produces a spectrum full of spikes. These evenly spaced frequencies are simplified numbers for teaching. Because the vocal folds are held in place along their edges, they **behave like a string**, so their harmonics are evenly spaced.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method** depends on **very clear statements about how the world works**, usually written as **differential equations**. **Solving those equations gives a prediction** about what a measurement will show.
children: The spring equations are one example. Solving them predicts that a spring that is pulled goes back, and a spring that is pushed also goes back.

The equations for the vocal folds are the same type as the spring equations. There are just many more of them, and they are a little more complicated. The principles of masses and springs are therefore enough to reason about the vocal folds.
The **theory** is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**. So when they vibrate, their spectrum should have **evenly spaced peaks**, which are called **harmonics**.
The **prediction** is that **when anyone's voice is measured at the larynx, its spectrum will have equidistant harmonics**, which means harmonics that are evenly spaced.

teaching.text: This prediction was tested by recording two voices in **Praat**, a program for analyzing speech. Each speaker held the **mouth wide open**, so no particular vowel was being made.
children: First voice: The lowest spike was near **100 hertz**. The next spikes were close to two, three, four and five times that value, so they were **evenly spaced, just as predicted**.
Second voice: The lowest spike was near **220 hertz**. The next spikes were near two and three times that value, so they were also evenly spaced, but farther apart.
**The prediction was correct for both voices.** A theory built from simple masses and springs made a precise, correct prediction about real speech.

teaching.text: The second voice has a **higher pitch**, so that speaker's vocal folds are probably **smaller and thinner**. **Thinner folds have less mass, and less mass means a higher frequency**, so all the harmonics are spaced farther apart.
children: This is part of how listeners **recognize people by their voices**. Each person's vocal folds give their voice its own spectrum, and getting to know someone's voice includes getting used to that spectrum.
Twins have the same genes and similar vocal folds, so they can be hard to tell apart on the phone.
How a person says particular vowels also matters. But vowels depend on the vibration of the **air** above the vocal folds, not on the folds themselves.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A string can also be **fixed at one end and free at the other**, just like a **building**, which is fixed to the ground and free to sway at the top. The **fixed bottom** cannot move, so every mode has a point of **no motion** there, which is called a **node**. The **free top** moves the most, and that point is called an **antinode**.
**In this kind of system, only the odd harmonics occur.** So the modes come at **100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz**, which are one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency.
children: **Mode 1** goes from no motion at the bottom to the most motion at the top, like a building swaying as a whole.
Two copies of Mode 1 would put a still point at both ends. That would make the system **fixed at both ends**, so this pattern cannot happen here.
**Three copies** do end with motion at the top. So the next mode has three times the frequency of Mode 1, and the mode after that has five copies.
The simple version is that the top must always be moving, and only an odd number of copies ends with motion at the top.

teaching.text: When **both ends are fixed**, a string has **every whole-number multiple** of the lowest frequency. When **one end is fixed and the other is free**, it has **only the odd multiples**.

**Civil engineers design buildings to sway only in Mode 1**, so every floor moves together. A building is not designed to be completely stiff, because buildings that cannot bend or move slightly are more likely to be damaged during an earthquake. Engineers also avoid the higher modes, because in those modes some floors would move one way while other floors moved the other way.

Compare two strings with the **same length and the same wave speed**. If one is fixed at both ends and the other is fixed at one end and free at the other, the fixed-free string has **half the lowest frequency**.
children: When all four fixed-free modes are equally strong, the spectrum measured at the free end has **four equal spikes** at the odd multiples.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: The **2026 Nobel Prize in economics** was awarded to **Robert Hall** and **Michael Woodford** for the **microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization**. **Stabilization** means returning a system to its equilibrium and keeping it there. This is the same role that **balancing feedback** plays, and the same role a spring plays when it pulls a mass back to rest.
children: In their model of the economy, **unemployment and inflation rise and fall in turn**, in the same way that the position and the velocity of a mass on a spring take turns.
The goal of stabilization policy is to **reduce the size of these rises and falls**, so the economy avoids very high unemployment and runaway inflation.

teaching.text: Woodford's theory is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**. Each part of the name describes one feature of the model.
children: Dynamic: The economy changes over time according to rules.

Stochastic: The model can handle **random shocks**, such as the start of a war or a large company's CEO being caught embezzling. This is similar to stochastic gradient descent, where one unusual data point can push the estimate far off, but later data pull it back toward the average.
Equilibrium: The goal is a steady state without large, sudden jumps.

teaching.text: **Macroeconomic** and **microeconomic** describe two levels of the same economy.
children: Macroeconomic: These quantities describe a whole economy, such as the inflation rate or the number of people who are unemployed.
Microeconomic: These events are single choices, such as one person buying something.

Explaining large patterns from many small events is the same kind of problem as speech. In speech, many small vibrations in the vocal tract add up to words that a listener understands without noticing any single vibration.

sections.title: One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass-spring system vibrates because **the spring tends to return to equilibrium**, while **a moving mass tends to keep moving**. The vibration can occur in two directions, and both behave in the same way.
children: Longitudinal motion: The mass moves back and forth along the line of the spring.
Transverse motion: The mass moves up and down between two walls, across the line of the springs.
Both directions are useful, because transverse motion is the easier way to understand the vocal folds, while longitudinal motion is the easier way to understand the air in the vocal tract.

teaching.text: **A part changes the frequency only while it is doing its job.** A mass changes the frequency only when it moves, and a spring changes the frequency only when it is stretched or compressed. This one principle explains every result about modes.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Mass and stiffness change the frequency in opposite directions.**
children: Mass: Increasing the mass lowers the frequency, so the system completes fewer cycles per second. A heavier mass is harder to turn around.
Stiffness: Increasing the stiffness raises the frequency, so the system completes more cycles per second. A stiffer spring pulls back with more force.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: A system with **two masses** has **two modes** (ways of vibrating), and it can also vibrate in both at once.
children: Mode 1: The masses move together. The middle spring is carried along without being stretched, so in practice the system uses **only two springs**, and the frequency is **lower**.
Mode 2: The masses move against each other. All **three springs** are stretched and compressed, which adds **stiffness** and gives a **higher frequency**.

teaching.text: Making the **middle spring stiffer** affects the two modes differently.
children: Mode 1: The frequency **does not change**, because the middle spring is never stretched in this mode.
Mode 2: The frequency **rises**, because the middle spring is stretched and compressed throughout this mode.
A spring therefore matters only in a mode where it is being stretched or compressed.

teaching.text: In real systems, the masses usually rise and fall together while also moving against each other, so **both modes occur at once**.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: A system with **three masses** has **three modes**.
children: Mode 1: All three masses move together.
Mode 2: The middle mass stays still while the two outer masses move against each other.
Mode 3: The middle mass moves against both outer masses.

teaching.text: Making **Mass 2**, the middle mass, heavier affects only the modes in which that mass moves.
children: Mode 1 and Mode 3: The frequency **goes down**, because the middle mass moves in both modes.
Mode 2: The frequency **does not change**, because the middle mass does not move in this mode.
**A mass affects the frequency only through its movement.** A mass that does not move has no effect, a mass that moves a little has a small effect, and a mass that moves a lot has a large effect.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: **Each added mass adds one more mode**, and the same patterns repeat as the chain gets longer.
children: Mode 1: Everything moves together.
Mode 2: The system splits into **two parts** that move against each other. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
Mode 3: The system splits into **three parts**, with the middle moving one way and the two sides moving the other way.

teaching.text: Adding more and more masses and springs produces a **string**. **Every small piece of a string has weight, which is its mass, and every small piece resists being stretched or compressed, which is its springiness.**
children: The same three mode patterns appear in a string.
Higher modes have more parts moving against each other, so the string is stretched and compressed more, and those modes vibrate faster.
In musical instruments, these frequencies are heard as **notes**. The ear can pick out many instruments at once because the ear itself is built from masses and springs.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends with its first mode at **100 hertz** has its next modes at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**. Every mode is an **exact multiple** of the first, and these multiples are called **harmonics**.
children: The second mode contains **two** copies of the first mode's bump, the third contains **three**, and the fifth contains **five**. Each mode's frequency is therefore the first frequency multiplied by the number of copies.

teaching.text: A single mode on its own produces a **pure tone**, which sounds so harsh that it is used for sirens. Everyday sounds contain many modes at once, which is why a real string's motion looks irregular, much like the waveform of speech.

A **spectrum** shows this mixture. **Frequency** is on the horizontal axis, and **amplitude** (strength) is on the vertical axis. For this string, the spectrum has spikes at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: All of the results so far follow from a short list of **principles of mass-spring systems**, and the principles are consistent with each other.
children: Mass and stiffness: **Increasing the mass lowers the frequency, and increasing the stiffness raises the frequency.**
Number of modes: **A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency.
Added mass: **Adding mass at a location lowers the frequency more when that location moves more.** How much a location moves depends on where it is.
Motion and stretching: **Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement.**
Added stiffness: **Adding stiffness at a location raises the frequency more when that location is stretched and compressed more.** This also depends on where the location is.

Fixed-fixed and fixed-free: In a **fixed-fixed system** (fixed at both ends), the harmonics are **whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency**, because each mode contains a whole number of copies of the lowest mode. In a **fixed-free system** (fixed at one end and free at the other), they are **odd multiples**, because each mode contains an odd number of copies.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Making one piece of a string **heavier**, such as thickening its exact middle, changes some modes and not others.
children: Mode 1: The middle moves a lot, so the added mass **lowers** the frequency.
Mode 2: The middle does not move, so the added mass has **no effect**.
Mode 3: The middle moves again, so the frequency goes down.
Mode 4: The middle is still again, so the frequency does not change. Moving up through the modes, the effect **alternates**.

teaching.text: **Along a vibrating string, locations of motion and locations of stretching alternate.** Where a piece moves the most, it is carried up and down and is hardly stretched. Where the string is stretched the most, such as right next to a fixed end, there is **no movement**.
children: **A useful shortcut is that the springiest locations are the locations that do not move.** In **Mode 5** of a string fixed at both ends, the string does not move at the **two fixed ends** or at the **four points where it crosses its middle line**, so those **six locations** are the springiest.
The **most motion**, and therefore the **least springiness**, occurs at the tops of the **five bumps**.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: Changing one small piece of a string can move two modes in **opposite directions**. Consider a location where **Mode 4 moves the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 does not move there. Both **mass** and **stiffness** are added to that piece.
children: Mode 4: The piece is moving, so the added mass **lowers** the frequency. The piece is barely stretched, so the added stiffness has no effect.
Mode 5: The piece is not moving, so the added mass has no effect. The piece is stretched the most, so the added stiffness **raises** the frequency.
The same change therefore **lowers Mode 4's frequency and raises Mode 5's frequency**. Each mode is worked out separately by asking whether the location is moving or stretching in that mode.

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates. In the late nineteenth century, researchers tested this by placing small amounts of **wax** on different parts of a **drum**.
children: When wax was placed where the drum vibrated a lot, the extra mass made the drum vibrate more slowly, causing its frequency (pitch) to **decrease**.
When wax was placed where the drum did not vibrate, it had **no effect** on the drum's frequency or sound.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The **larynx** contains the **vocal folds**, which form a **membrane** (a thin sheet of tissue) similar to a drum. Like a drum, the vocal folds have many modes of vibration.
children: Mode 1: All the masses move up and down together.
Mode 2: The two halves move against each other.
Higher modes: The surface divides into more and more parts.
The vocal folds are fixed around their edges, so they behave like a fixed-fixed system, and their frequencies are harmonics (whole-number multiples of the lowest one).

teaching.text: Changes to the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds change the voice. Heavy smokers can develop **nodules** (small growths) on the vocal folds. A nodule adds mass at one location and changes the stiffness of the tissue around it, so the folds vibrate differently and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **theory** predicts that the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, so a measured voice should have a spectrum with **equidistant harmonics** (harmonics that are evenly spaced). A voice was recorded and analyzed in **Praat**. Its lowest harmonic was about 130 hertz, and the next harmonics were close to two and three times that value, so **the measurement matched the prediction.**
children: This is how the **scientific method** works. A clear theory is written as **differential equations**, the equations are solved to produce a prediction, and the prediction is checked against a measurement.
Each person's lowest frequency is different, but the harmonics above it are always close to multiples of it.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed at one end and free at the other**. The base is fixed to the ground, while the top can sway in strong winds or an earthquake. Engineers design a building to sway only in **Mode 1**. That motion can feel unpleasant on a high floor, but it is safe. Swaying in a higher mode could break the building.
The **air inside the vocal tract** is also a fixed-free system.
children: Glottis end: The **vocal folds are closed**, so the air there **cannot move**, and that end is **fixed**.
Lip end: The air can move in and out freely, so that end is **free**.
Unlike a building, the air in the vocal tract vibrates in **all of its modes**. Speaking changes the mass and stiffness of the air at different locations along the tract.

teaching.text: A fixed-free system has **frequencies at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz**, which are only the odd multiples of 100. The first mode goes from **no motion** at the fixed end to **maximum motion** at the free end, which is one quarter of a wave. The next possible modes contain **three** and then **five** of these quarter-wave pieces.
children: Two pieces would end with no motion at both ends, which is the pattern of a fixed-fixed system, so even multiples never occur.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **chain of masses and springs** that is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips. The masses represent the air's tendency to keep moving, and the springs represent the air's springiness.
children: First formant: The lowest mode corresponds to the **first formant**, **F1**.
Second formant: The next mode corresponds to the **second formant**, **F2**. It vibrates **three times faster** than the first mode, because it contains three of the first mode's quarter-wave pieces.
The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**, while the frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are called harmonics.

teaching.text: Three locations along the tube are important for vowels.
children: /a/: The constriction is **one-third of the way from the glottis**.
/i/: The constriction is **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**.
/u/: The constriction is at the **free end, at the lips**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** (narrowing) is a location where the tongue or lips narrow the vocal tract. Its position is measured from the **glottis**, the space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
children: Done: There is **no significant constriction** in the vocal tract, so this is the central vowel.
Dean: The constriction occurs under the roof of the mouth, about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, producing a **high front** vowel.
Don: The constriction occurs far back in the throat, about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, producing a **low back** vowel.
Dune: The constriction occurs **at the lips** because of **lip rounding**, producing a **high back** vowel.
Dan: The tongue is positioned low and toward the front of the mouth, producing a **low front** vowel.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **A constriction increases both the stiffness and the mass of the air.**
children: Stiffness: Compressed air becomes **stiffer**, in the same way that the air in a tire becomes stiffer when it is compressed.
Mass: Packing air into a smaller space raises its **density**, which makes it more **massive**.

teaching.text: It might seem that raising mass and stiffness together would **cancel out**. **That is false** for any system with many masses and springs, because in a given mode each location is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching**.
children: Location with no motion and a lot of stretching: Only the added stiffness matters, so the frequency **rises**.
Location with a lot of motion and no stretching: Only the added mass matters, so the frequency **falls**.
Speech itself proves that the effects do not cancel, because constrictions at different locations clearly change the frequencies of the voice.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, **lip rounding** creates a constriction at the **free end**, which raises the mass and the stiffness of the air there.
children: Mode 1: The air at the free end moves a lot and is hardly compressed, so **motion matters most**, and the added mass **lowers F1**.
Mode 2: The air at the free end also moves a lot, so **motion matters most** again, and the added mass **lowers F2**.
Result: **Both F1 and F2 go down** for /u/.

teaching.text: A speaker started from the central vowel, with formants near 500, 1500 and 2500 hertz, and moved into /u/. **Both formants dropped**, as predicted.
children: The rounded lips added mass where the air moves the most. The added stiffness had no effect there, because the air at the lips is moving, not stretching.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, and that one location behaves differently in the two modes.
children: Mode 1: The air at this location moves a lot and is hardly compressed, so **motion matters most**, and the added mass **lowers F1**.
Mode 2: The air at this location is strongly compressed, so **springiness matters most**, and the added stiffness **raises F2**.
Result: One formant falls while the other rises, because the same constriction is at a location of motion for F1 and at a location of compression for F2.

teaching.text: A speaker went from the central vowel into /i/. The **first formant dropped sharply**, and the **second formant rose**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, and the pattern is reversed.
children: Mode 1: This location is near the fixed end, where the air is strongly compressed, so **springiness matters most**, and the added stiffness **raises F1**.
Mode 2: The air at this location moves a lot, so **motion matters most**, and the added mass **lowers F2**.
Result: **F1 goes up and F2 goes down**, so the two formants move closer together.

teaching.text: The reasoning also works in reverse.
children: Large rise: **If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air at that location must be springy and hardly moving in that mode.**
Large fall: **If a constriction lowers a formant a lot, the air at that location must be moving a lot.**

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The same principles explain all the vowels. **Added mass matters where the air moves, and added stiffness matters where the air is compressed and expanded.** The vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, so its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air in the tube can be modeled as **lines of air particles**, where each particle represents billions of real air molecules. The closed vocal folds are at the **fixed end**, and the open lips are at the **free end**.
children: Compression and expansion: Where the lines crowd together and then spread apart, the air is **compressing and expanding**, which is **springiness**.
Motion: Where the lines move back and forth without changing their spacing, the air is acting as a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end**.

teaching.text: Each formant has a fixed number of points with no motion.
children: F1: There is one point of no motion, at the fixed end.
F2: There are two points of no motion.
F3: There are three points of no motion.
Between each pair of no-motion points, locations of maximum motion and locations of maximum compression alternate, as they do along a vibrating string.

teaching.text: For the **schwa**, which has no constriction, a measured voice had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**. These are the odd multiples that the theory predicts.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: The question **Where were you a year ago?** uses all of the constriction rules at once. Each sound places a constriction at a different location, so the formants move up and down continuously instead of staying at fixed values.
children: /i/-like sound: The tongue forms a constriction near the front of the mouth, so **F1 goes down and F2 goes up**. This location is a location of motion in Mode 1 and a location of compression in Mode 2.
you: **Lip rounding** forms a constriction at the lips, so **F1 and F2 both go down**. The air at the lips is moving in every mode.
/a/-like sound: The tongue moves back and down, so **F1 rises and F2 falls**. This location is a location of compression in Mode 1 and a location of motion in Mode 2.

teaching.text: **Speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.** The frequencies of the air in the vocal tract are always changing, and the same mass and spring principles predict which way each formant moves at every moment.

lecture13.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production · Source and Filter

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Every vibrating system in speech follows a small set of principles, and the principles are consistent with each other.
children: Mass and stiffness: **Increasing the mass lowers the frequency, and increasing the stiffness raises the frequency.**

Number of modes: **A system with n masses has n modes**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency. In higher modes, more parts move against each other, so more springs are stretched and compressed.

Location of a change: **Adding mass at a location lowers the frequency more when that location moves more.** **Adding stiffness at a location raises the frequency more when that location is stretched and compressed more.**
Motion and stretching: **Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement.**

Harmonics and formants: In a **fixed-fixed system** (fixed at both ends), the frequencies are called **harmonics**, and they are **whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency. In a **fixed-free system** (fixed at one end and free at the other), the frequencies are called **formants**, and they are **odd multiples**.

teaching.text: It might seem that raising both the mass and the stiffness of a system would make the two effects **cancel out**. That is true only for a **single mass on a single spring**. In a system with many masses and springs, a location that moves a lot is hardly stretched, and a location that is stretched a lot hardly moves, so only one of the two changes matters at any one location.
children: Picture a spot on a string that never moves but is strongly stretched. Added mass there has no effect, but added stiffness makes the string pull back harder, so the frequency goes up.
Picture a spot that moves up and down the most. Added stiffness there has no effect, but added mass makes that spot harder to move, so the frequency goes down.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Adding masses adds modes, and the same mode shapes keep repeating.
children: Mode 1: Everything moves together.
Mode 2: The system splits into two halves that move against each other.
Mode 3: The middle moves against the sides.

The more the parts move against each other, the more the springs are stretched and compressed, so **higher modes are stiffer and vibrate faster**. A higher mode does not use stiffer springs. It makes the same springs stretch more.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: In a string fixed at both ends, the first mode is **one half-wave**, a single bump that goes from no motion at one end, to maximum motion in the middle, to no motion at the other end. Each higher mode fits **more of these half-wave pieces** into the same length.
children: Mode 2: The mode **contains two pieces**, with one half moving up while the other half moves down. Each piece behaves like a copy of Mode 1, so Mode 2 has **twice the stiffness** and **twice the frequency**.
Mode 3 and Mode 5: Mode 3 **contains three pieces**, and Mode 5 **contains five**, so the fifth mode has five times the frequency of the first.
Exam answer: **The fifth mode contains five copies of the first mode**, so it has five times the stiffness and five times the frequency.

teaching.text: The numbers do not have to start at 100. A voice whose lowest frequency is **250 hertz** has its next harmonics at 500, 750 and 1000 hertz, because each harmonic is still a whole number of copies of the first.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in all of these modes at once. Its **spectrum** has **evenly spaced spikes**, one for each harmonic. **Frequency** is on the horizontal axis, and **amplitude** (strength) is on the vertical axis. If the first harmonic is 100 hertz, the next ones are 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.
children: The **vocal folds** are fixed on all sides, just behind the Adam's apple, so they behave like a fixed-fixed system and produce harmonics.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The vocal folds form a **membrane** (a thin sheet of tissue), and the same counting of pieces works on a surface.
children: First mode: A single bump spans the whole membrane.
Second mode: Two bumps fit across the membrane, so the frequency is twice as high.
Fourth mode: Four ups and downs fit across the membrane, so the frequency is four times as high.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed at the base** and **free at the top**. In strong winds or an earthquake, engineers want it to sway only in **Mode 1**, with every floor moving together. That motion can feel unpleasant on a high floor, but it is safe. In a higher mode, some floors would move one way while other floors moved the other way, and the building could break apart.

A string can be set up the same way, fixed at the bottom and free at the top. Its first mode is no longer a full half-wave. It goes from **no motion at the fixed end** to **maximum motion at the free end**, which is only **one quarter of a wave**.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: In a fixed-free system, each mode is built from **quarter-wave packets** (pieces that are each a quarter of a wave long). Each packet runs from no motion to maximum motion.
children: Mode 1: The mode contains one packet.
Mode 2: The mode contains three packets.
Mode 3: The mode contains five packets.
Mode 4: The mode contains seven packets. With a lowest mode of 100 hertz, the modes are therefore at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz.

teaching.text: **Two packets can never fit.** Two quarter-wave packets would go from no motion, to maximum motion, to no motion again. That would place a point of no motion at the top as well as the bottom, which would make the system **fixed at both ends**. Adding one more packet, for **three** in total, ends with maximum motion at the top again, so three is the next possible mode.
children: In short, the free end must always be moving, and only an odd number of quarter-wave packets ends with motion at the free end.

teaching.text: The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**. **A formant is a frequency at which a system vibrates when it is fixed at one end and completely free at the other.** Formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one, and they are written **F1**, **F2** and **F3**.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: Counting quarter-wave packets gives every formant from the first one.
children: F1: The first formant is **500 hertz**.
F2: The second formant is **three times F1, which is 1500 hertz**.
F3: The third formant is **five times F1, which is 2500 hertz**.
Each step from one formant to the next is twice the first formant, because each new mode adds two more quarter-wave packets.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air inside the mouth and throat forms a tube with two different ends.
children: Glottis end: The **vocal folds** are closed, so the air there **cannot move back and forth**, and that end is **fixed**.
Lip end: The **lips are open**, so the air can move back and forth freely, and that end is **free**.
Comparison: **The air in the vocal tract vibrates the same way a building sways.** The mathematics for both is almost identical, and the frequencies of both are **formants**.
Speaking changes the stiffness and mass of the air at different locations in the tract. That moves the formants, which is how listeners hear different vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air in the tube can be modeled as lines of particles, where each particle represents billions of air molecules.
children: Spring behavior: Where the lines **crowd together and then spread far apart**, the air is compressing and expanding, so it is acting like a **spring**.
Mass behavior: Where the lines **move back and forth** without changing their spacing, the air is acting like a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end, at the lips**.
Crowding and spreading indicate springiness, and sliding without crowding indicates mass.

teaching.text: The modes of the air match the modes of a building.
children: Mode 1: The only point of no motion is the fixed end.
Mode 2: There are **two** points of no motion.
Mode 3: There are **three** points of no motion. Around each of these points, the air is strongly compressed and expanded.

teaching.text: In **Mode 4** of a building, **the springiest locations are the fixed base and the three points where the building crosses its resting position**, four locations in all. These locations are the springiest because they do not move.
children: Adding stiffness where the building moves the most **changes nothing**, because the building is not acting like a spring there. Adding stiffness where the building does not move makes the frequency **rise sharply**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** (narrowing) is a location where the tongue or lips narrow the vocal tract. Its position is measured from the **glottis**, the space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
children: Done: There is **no significant constriction**, so this is the central vowel.
Dean: The constriction occurs under the roof of the mouth, about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, producing a **front high vowel**.
Don: The constriction occurs far back in the throat, about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, producing a **low back vowel**.
Dune: The constriction occurs **at the lips** because of **lip rounding**, producing a **back high vowel**.
Dan: The tongue is positioned low and toward the front of the mouth, producing a **front low vowel**.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: A constriction changes the air in two ways at once.
children: Stiffness: **Compressing air raises its stiffness**, just as compressing the air in a tire makes it stiffer. A constriction where the air is strongly compressed therefore **raises the frequency**.
Mass: **Packing air together raises its mass**, because it raises the air's **density**. A constriction where the air moves a lot therefore **lowers the frequency**.

teaching.text: Every constriction **adds both mass and stiffness**, but the effects do not cancel out. **Along a vibrating string or a vibrating column of air, the locations that move the most alternate with the locations that are compressed and expanded the most.**
children: Any constriction question can be answered in two steps. First, determine whether the air at that location is mostly moving or mostly being compressed in the mode in question. Second, decide whether the added mass or the added stiffness matters there.

teaching.text: The same two steps answer a question about a string fixed at both ends. Consider a small spot where **Mode 3 crosses its middle line** and **Mode 4 is at the top of a bump**, and add both mass and stiffness to that spot.
children: Mode 3: The string does not move at that spot but is stretched the most, so only the added stiffness matters, and **Mode 3's frequency goes up**.
Mode 4: The string moves the most at that spot and is hardly stretched, so only the added mass matters, and **Mode 4's frequency goes down**.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Before reasoning about any vowel, it helps to know where the air moves and where it is compressed in the first two modes.
children: Mode 1: The air near the closed glottis end is strongly compressed and expanded, while the air near the open lip end mostly moves back and forth.
Mode 2: The air is strongly compressed at the closed end and again about two-thirds of the way along. In between, about one-third of the way along, the air mostly moves.

Rule for the ends: **In every mode, the air at the closed end is always springy, and the air at the open end is always moving.** Air can be compressed against a closed end, but at an open end there is nothing to compress it against.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The mass-spring chain marks the three vowel locations along the tube.
children: /a/: The constriction is **one-third of the way from the glottis**.
/i/: The constriction is **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**.
/u/: The constriction is at the **lip end**.
Each vowel adds mass and stiffness at its own location, and its effect on F1 and F2 depends on whether the air there is moving or being compressed in each mode.

teaching.text: Adding mass and stiffness at the **very top of a building** lowers the frequency of **every mode**, including Mode 4. The top is the free end, so in every mode it moves the most and is hardly stretched, and only the added mass matters there.
children: **The top of the building corresponds to the lip end of the vocal tract.** This is why lip rounding lowers every formant.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, **lip rounding** creates a constriction at the **free end**. In both Mode 1 and Mode 2, the air at the free end moves a lot and is hardly compressed. The added **mass** therefore matters in both modes, and **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: A speaker moved from the central vowel into /u/, and the recording showed **both formants dropping**, as predicted.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**.
children: Mode 1: The air at that location moves a lot, so the added mass matters and **F1 goes down**.
Mode 2: The air at that location is strongly compressed, so the added stiffness matters and **F2 goes up**.
Measurement: A speaker moved from the central vowel into /i/. The **first formant dropped sharply**, and the **second formant rose**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, which reverses the /i/ pattern.
children: Mode 1: That location is near the fixed end, where the air is strongly compressed, so the added stiffness matters and **F1 goes up**.
Mode 2: The air at that location moves a lot, so the added mass matters and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The reasoning also works in reverse.
children: Large rise: **If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air at that location must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode.**
Large fall: **If a constriction lowers a formant a lot, the air at that location must be moving a lot.**

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: A **schwa** is produced with no constriction. A measured schwa had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, which are the odd multiples that a uniform fixed-free tube predicts. Every other vowel moves the formants away from these values by changing where the air moves and where it is compressed.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: Speech uses **two vibrating systems at the same time**.
children: Source: The **vocal folds** are a fixed-fixed system, so they produce **harmonics**. The lowest harmonic is called the **base frequency**, or **F0**. In this example, the harmonics are **100 hertz apart**.
Filter: The **air in the vocal tract** is a fixed-free system, so its frequencies are the **formants**. For the schwa, the formants are near **500, 1500, 2500 and 3500 hertz**.

teaching.text: **The formants determine how tall the harmonics are.** All the harmonics are still present, but **harmonics near a formant are tall, and harmonics far from any formant are short**. The outline of their heights is called the **envelope**, and it rises to a peak at each formant.
children: **The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel. Only their heights change, and the envelope is what makes each vowel sound different.**
In other words, the vocal folds determine which frequencies are present, and the shape of the vocal tract determines which of those frequencies are loud.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the filter keeps **F1 low and F2 high**. The tall harmonics are grouped at the very bottom of the spectrum, a long stretch of short harmonics follows, and the next tall group appears much higher up. The two lowest formants are therefore **far apart**.
children: The constriction two-thirds of the way from the glottis produces this pattern, because it lowers F1 and raises F2.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the filter **raises F1 and lowers F2**, so the first two groups of tall harmonics are **close together** in the lower part of the spectrum.
children: The same harmonics from the vocal folds are present under both /i/ and /a/, and only the filter differs. Moving the constriction moves the formants, and that changes which harmonics are loud.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: **A spectrum describes one instant**, but speech is **time-varying** (it changes over time), because the vocal tract keeps moving and constrictions keep forming and releasing. **A spectrogram places many spectra side by side over time.**
children: Time: Time is on the **horizontal axis**.
Frequency: Frequency, which was on the horizontal axis of each spectrum, is now on the **vertical axis**.
Amplitude: Amplitude, which was the height of each spike, is now shown as **darkness**. The louder a frequency is, the darker it appears.

teaching.text: The formants appear as **dark bands** that move as the speaker moves. In **/ia/**, the two lowest bands start **far apart** during /i/. As the speaker moves into /a/, **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the bands **come close together**.
children: Reading a spectrogram means following the dark bands, because those bands are the formants changing over time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **Where were you a year ago?** is a useful sentence for seeing the source and the filter working together over time.
children: Source: The vocal folds keep producing harmonics throughout the sentence.
Filter: The vocal tract keeps changing shape, so the envelope over the harmonics changes from moment to moment.
Spectrogram: These changes appear as **dark bands that rise and fall**, because the dark bands are the formants and darkness shows amplitude.
/i/-like vowel: The two lowest bands spread far apart.
you: All the bands drop, because lip rounding forms a constriction at the lips.

teaching.text: **A spectrum shows one frozen instant, but a spectrogram shows how the formants move**, and real speech is always moving. Reading a sentence like this one means following each band and asking which constriction moved it.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants can only appear through the harmonics, so the spacing of the harmonics matters.
children: Close harmonics: With harmonics every **100 hertz** and formants at **300 and 2100 hertz**, **many harmonics** sit under each formant peak, so the formants are easy to see.

Wide harmonics: With a higher base frequency, such as **250 hertz**, fewer harmonics land on each formant peak, and a formant can fall **between two harmonics**. It then becomes **very hard to tell the harmonics apart from the formants**.
Examples: A **toddler's** harmonics can be at 400, 800 and 1200 hertz, and a **soprano's** can start at 800 hertz. That is why their vowels can be very hard to identify.

teaching.text: **The formants form a smooth outline, and the harmonics are single points along that outline.** A higher F0 means fewer points, so the spectrogram no longer shows clean formant bands.
children: The harmonics work like dots used to trace a curve. With many dots, the curve is obvious, and with only a few dots, the curve is hard to see.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: Speech uses **two main vibrating systems**. The first is the **vocal folds**, a **membrane** (a thin sheet of tissue) that is **fixed on all sides** and made of many masses and springs. The vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, and all of the modes add together into one combined motion.
children: Mode 1: All the masses move up and down together.
Mode 2: Half of the masses move up while the other half move down.
Higher modes: The patterns become more and more complicated.

The vocal folds are a fixed-fixed system, so their frequencies are **harmonics** (whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency). The **lowest harmonic** is called **F0**. Each person has a different F0, but the other harmonics are always multiples of it.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: The second system is the **air in the vocal tract**.
children: Glottis end: The air is **fixed** there, because the closed vocal folds prevent it from moving back and forth.
Lip end: The air is **free** there, because it can move in and out of the open lips.
Because one end is fixed and the other is free, only the **odd multiples** occur, so the frequencies are one, three, five and seven times the lowest one.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: Each fixed-free mode is built from **quarter-wavelength packets** (pieces that are each a quarter of a wave long). Each packet runs from no motion at one point to maximum motion at another.
children: Mode 1: The mode contains one packet.
Mode 2: The mode contains three packets.
Mode 3: The mode contains five packets.
Mode 4: The mode contains seven packets.
Two packets would end with a point of no motion at the free end, which cannot happen. Only odd numbers of packets fit, which is why the formants are odd multiples of the first.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: In the vocal tract, the air moves **longitudinally**, which means back and forth along the tube rather than up and down. Each formant is one mode of this back-and-forth motion. F1 is the lowest mode, and F2 is the next one.
children: These modes look like a building's modes turned on their side, with the fixed glottis end on the left and the free lip end on the right.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: **In every mode, the air at the closed end is always springy, and the air at the open end is always moving.** Air can be compressed against a closed end, but at an open end there is nothing to compress it against.
children: Closed end: The thin layers of air crowd together and then spread far apart, so the air **compresses and expands** and acts like a **spring**.
Open end: The layers stay the same distance apart and move back and forth together, so the air acts like a **mass**.
Comparison: The lip end swings like a heavy door, and the throat end compresses like a pillow.

teaching.text: In higher modes, springy locations and moving locations **alternate** more and more times along the tube.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: The effect of a constriction can be worked out at any location, in any mode, with the same steps. Consider a location inside the tube where, in **Mode 3**, the layers of air crowd together and spread apart but hardly move back and forth. A constriction at that location raises **F3**.
children: Step 1: A constriction always **adds both mass and stiffness** to the air, just as compressing the air in a tire makes it stiffer.
Step 2: At this location in Mode 3, the air is acting like a **pure spring**. It is compressed and expanded but does not move back and forth, so the added mass does not matter.
Step 3: Only the added stiffness matters, and **increased stiffness raises the frequency**, so **F3 goes up**.

teaching.text: The answer should not be memorized. It should be **built one step at a time**, with each step based on the one before it. Good arguments in science and in art are built the same way.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Images taken while people speak show where constrictions (narrowings) occur in the vocal tract, which extends from the closed glottis to the open lips.
children: Done: There is no significant constriction in the vocal tract.
Dean: The constriction occurs near the front of the vocal tract, about two-thirds of the way from the glottis.
Don: The constriction occurs toward the back of the throat, about one-third of the way from the glottis.
Dune: The constriction occurs at the lips because of lip rounding.
Dan: The tongue is positioned low and toward the front of the mouth, producing a low front vowel.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A constriction changes two properties of the air.
children: Mass: A constriction increases the air's **mass**, which is how hard the air is to start or stop moving.
Stiffness: A constriction increases the air's **stiffness**, which is how strongly the air pushes back when it is compressed.
In the mass-spring model, a constriction is drawn as **heavier masses and stiffer springs** at that location.

teaching.text: A constriction always raises both, but moving locations and springy locations alternate along the tube, so **its effect depends on what the air is doing at that location in each mode**.
children: **When stiffness is what matters at a location, the frequency goes up. When mass is what matters, the frequency goes down.**

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: The same location in the tube can behave differently in the two modes, so each mode has to be checked separately. A location can be a location of motion in Mode 1 and a location of compression in Mode 2. One constriction at that location then lowers F1 and raises F2 at the same time.
children: That is why a vowel is defined by its pair of formants, not by one formant alone.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, **lip rounding** creates a constriction at the lips. At the open end, the air moves back and forth and is hardly compressed in **every** mode, so it acts like a pure mass. The added stiffness has no effect, but the added mass does, so **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: The schwa's formants are about **500 and 1500 hertz**. A measured /u/ had an F1 in the low two hundreds, well below 500.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is about two-thirds of the way from the glottis.
children: Mode 1: The air at that location moves back and forth, so it acts like a mass. The added mass matters, and **F1 goes down**.
Mode 2: The air at that location is compressed and expanded, so it acts like a spring. The added stiffness matters, and **F2 goes up**.
Measurement: A speaker moving from the schwa into /i/ produced exactly this pattern, with **F1 going down and F2 going up**.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is about one-third of the way from the glottis.
children: Mode 1: That location is close to the closed end, so the air there is mostly springy. The added stiffness matters, and **F1 goes up**.
Mode 2: That location lies between two springy regions, so the air there is mostly moving. The added mass matters, and **F2 goes down**.
Measurement: A speaker producing /a/ showed **F1 going up and F2 going down**. In a typical /a/, F1 and F2 are fairly close together.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The same reasoning applies to all three vowels. **First, determine whether the air at the constriction is mostly moving or mostly being compressed in each mode. Then decide whether the added mass or the added stiffness matters.**
children: /u/: The constriction is at the lips, where the air is moving in both modes, so both formants go down.
/i/: The constriction is two-thirds of the way along, where the air is moving in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2, so F1 goes down and F2 goes up.
/a/: The constriction is one-third of the way along, where the air is springy in Mode 1 and moving in Mode 2, so F1 goes up and F2 goes down.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds are the **source**. Their mass and stiffness set **F0**, and F0 sets the spacing of the harmonics.
children: Large, heavy, loose vocal folds: They have high mass and low stiffness, so **F0 is low**, around 100 hertz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
Tighter, lighter vocal folds: F0 is higher, for example 250 hertz.
Very tight, light vocal folds: F0 is higher still, for example 350 hertz.

teaching.text: **F0 does not stay constant while people talk.** Speakers keep changing F0 by tightening and loosening their vocal folds, and listeners use those changes to understand meaning.
children: Statement: When **The dog slept here** is said as a statement, F0 falls at the very end.
Question: When the same words are said as a question, F0 rises at the end.
The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a speaker is being sarcastic, pretending, or even lying.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract is the **filter**, and its formants depend on **where the constriction is**.
children: Schwa: F1 is near 500 hertz and F2 is near 1500 hertz.
/u/: Both formants are lower.
/i/: F1 and F2 are very far apart.
/a/: F1 and F2 are very close together.

teaching.text: **The core rule is that a formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder, and harmonics far from any formant are weaker.**
children: **The vowel shape is the filter. The vocal folds supply the harmonics, and the filter determines which harmonics come through strongly.**

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **The lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants can shape.** When the harmonics are 100 hertz apart, many harmonics sit under each formant, so the spectrum clearly shows the formant peaks.

With very light, tight vocal folds, a formant at 500 hertz may have **no harmonic near it to strengthen**. With so few harmonics, a formant can fall between them and be missed, or its position can be hard to identify.
children: Opera singer: This is an extreme case, which is why sung vowels are hard to identify. Singers are even trained to shape the vocal tract so that the formants line up with the harmonics.
Small child: A small child has an F0 near 500 hertz, so very few harmonics fall near the formants. That is why only the people who care for the child understand the child's speech easily.
The formants are the same in every case, but a high voice gives the listener only a few harmonics through which to hear them.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** places many spectra side by side over time.
children: Time: Time is on the horizontal axis.
Frequency: Frequency is on the vertical axis.
Amplitude: **Darkness** shows how much energy, or amplitude, is present.

teaching.text: F0 can be measured in **Praat** by selecting a short stretch of speech, viewing its spectrum, and identifying the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had an F0 of about 170 hertz, and the next harmonic was at about twice that value.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: The sentence **Where were you a year ago?** brings every idea about speech together. The vocal folds supply harmonics the whole time, and each new sound changes where the tongue and lips form a constriction, so the formants keep moving from one moment to the next.
children: Spectrogram: **Time** is on the horizontal axis, **frequency** is on the vertical axis, and the **dark bands are the formants**.
/i/-like vowel: **F2 rises high and F1 stays low**, because the constriction is at a location that is springy in Mode 2 and moving in Mode 1.
you: The formants **drop**, because lip rounding adds mass where the air moves the most, and that lowers all of them.
a year ago: F2 goes up and then down again as the tongue moves from one vowel to the next.

teaching.text: **The formants are always changing during speech, so speech is not a sequence of frozen vowels.** Every rise and fall of a formant can be predicted with the same mass and spring reasoning, by identifying the location of the constriction and whether the air there is moving or being compressed in each mode.
children: This constant change is why a network that sees two formants from one frozen moment cannot understand real speech. Speech recognition requires systems that take in whole stretches of sound over time.
A spectrogram of a real sentence is a continuous record of the tongue and lips, and reading it means following the dark bands as they rise and fall.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: A recording that was cut and joined back together shows how complex speech perception is. The **m** portion of a recorded **ma** was joined to the **a** portion of a recorded **na**, and listeners clearly heard **na**, not ma.
children: **Whether listeners hear m or n depends more on the vowel than on the nasal sound itself.**
After m: One formant of the vowel stays fairly **flat**.
After n: That formant shows a **big drop**.

Listeners therefore decide which consonant they heard **during the vowel**, after the consonant has ended. This was one of the first striking results in speech perception, published in the **1950s** by the linguist **André Malécot**.

teaching.text: Listeners **take in whole stretches of speech and then decide** about the sounds that came first. For about seventy years, speech recognition systems that treated each slice of sound separately **failed**. Modern speech recognition uses large language models, which use what comes later to decide about what came before.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can be trained to recognize vowels from formants. Its **two inputs** are **F1 and F2**, measured from real recordings of five vowels, and its task is to decide which vowel was spoken.
children: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights**, and the weights are learned from the data.
Information enters at the input, somewhat like sound reaching the ear. Each hidden layer turns the numbers it receives into a new set of numbers, somewhat like the stages of processing in the brain.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The network has three parts.
children: Output layer: There are **five output neurons**, one for each word, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
Hidden layers: There are **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**.
Connections: Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is **fully connected**.
This version is **purely linear**, which means it has **no activation functions**. Each neuron simply passes on the result of its inner product.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between minus one and one**.
children: Positive weight: The input pushes the next neuron up.
Negative weight: The input pushes the next neuron down.
The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000 hertz**. A very low F1 with a very high F2 is the pattern of **/i/**, so the correct answer is **dean**.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network one layer at a time. Each neuron computes an **inner product**, which means it multiplies each incoming number by its weight and adds the results.
children: For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, F1 is multiplied by its weight, F2 is multiplied by its weight, and the two results are added. That sum is the neuron's activation.

The other neurons do the same with their own weights. The first hidden layer produces three numbers, which pass through the next weights to produce two numbers, then four, and then five at the output.
These calculations never have to be done by hand. What matters is that every step is an inner product.

teaching.text: The output is a **probability distribution** over the five words, with values of **.5, .1, .1, .1 and .2**, which add up to one. With random weights, the network gives its highest probability to **done**, so it is wrong.
children: The correct answer is given as the target distribution **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. **Stochastic gradient descent** then changes each weight so that next time the inner products give a high probability to dean.
The network starts out guessing, the target shows what the correct guess was, and learning adjusts every weight so the correct guess wins next time.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** describes the network as a list of layers.
children: Sequential: The network has **one layer after another, in order**.
Linear: The layer **computes inner products** of the weights and the activations from the previous layer.
nn.Linear(2, 3): The layer **takes input from 2 neurons and has 3 neurons**. The next lines read 3 in and 2 out, then 2 in and 4 out, then 4 in and 5 out.
Bias set to False: Every layer stays purely linear, which matches the diagram of the network.

teaching.text: **Only layers that perform calculations get a line of code.** The **input layer** has no incoming weights and computes no inner products, so it never gets its own line, and the first line describes the **first hidden layer**.
children: This network has **five layers in total** but only **three hidden layers**. The **last line is always the output layer**, so the question must be read carefully.

teaching.text: To **add a hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output**, the old last line, 4 in and 5 out, becomes **4 in and 3 out**, and a new last line takes **3 in and gives 5 out**.
children: Quick check: The first number on each line must match the second number on the line before it.

teaching.text: Consider a network written as 4 in and 3 out, 3 in and 8 out, 8 in and 4 out, 4 in and 4 out, and 4 in and 5 out.
children: Input: The network takes **4 numbers as input**.
Hidden layers: It has **four hidden layers** with 3, 8, 4 and 4 neurons.
Output: It chooses among **5 categories**. When the first category is correct, the target distribution has a **1 in the first slot and 0 everywhere else**.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: A **neural network** can work as a very simple **speech recognizer**. It takes the **two formants, F1 and F2**, of a vowel and decides which of **five words** it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**. Networks like this were used fifteen or twenty years ago. Modern **large language models** are built from many networks like this one, the way molecules are built from **atoms**.

The network has **2 input neurons**, **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**, and **5 output neurons**. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is **fully connected**.
children: Input neurons: The **input neurons** only take in numbers from outside the network. For example, one speaker's vowel might have an F1 of 400 and an F2 of 1900.

Weights: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights.** Each connection has a weight, which is a positive or negative number. The whole network is just a machine that processes numbers using those weights.
Activations: Each neuron's activation is calculated from the neurons that feed into it. The activations of the last layer become the network's decision.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs
